title: The Symposium — Part Two
subtitle: Pausanias divides Love in two. Aristophanes gets the hiccups.

customObject.name: the krater
customObject.description: the great wine-mixing bowl at the centre of the couches — still mostly for show

script.note: MAP: the_hallwyl_museum_1st_floor_combined — Agathon's dining room, later the same night. Phaedrus has spoken; the applause has settled. Pausanias rises, smooths his robe, and takes his time about it.

script.text: Phaedrus, that was stirring. It was also, forgive me, praise of the wrong god — or rather, of only half of one.
Half a god? Careful, Pausanias — they charge double for blasphemy after midnight.
Hear me out. We keep saying 'Love' as if it were one thing. It is two. And until you split them, every word said in Love's honour is confusion poured on confusion.

There is the common love. It aims at the body, and only at the body. It picks its target by convenience, it counts beauty like coins — and when the body changes, as bodies do, it is gone by morning. The common lover loves a purchase, not a person.

And there is the heavenly love. It aims at the mind — at character, at what a person is becoming. It arrives slowly, because minds open slowly. And it stays, because the thing it loves does not wrinkle. The heavenly lover is a gardener, gentlemen. The common lover is a shopper.
I've been both in one evening. Which god do I invoice?

script.note: Laughter around the couches. Pausanias waits it out, unbothered.

script.text: Laugh — but every city already legislates as if this were true. We praise lovers who stay through sickness and we sneer at ones who vanish after a night. The law inside people is already written. I am only reading it aloud.
So here is my praise: not of Love entire, but of the heavenly half. Love that makes both people better than they were. Any other kind is appetite wearing Love's cloak.

script.note: He sits. Solid applause — the argument has teeth, and everyone at the table knows they'll be chewing on it for years.

script.text: A doctor's note: he has just diagnosed half the room. I saw at least three of you check your own symptoms mid-speech.
A fine blade, Pausanias. Though I wonder — you split Love in two so cleanly. Has anyone ever met either half walking around alone? Or do they only exist in speeches? …Later. I'm promised to go last.
And next in order — Aristophanes! The funniest man in Athens, on the god of Love. We are either blessed or doomed, no third outcome.

script.note: Aristophanes stands, opens his mouth grandly — and hiccups. Loudly. He tries again. Worse.

script.text: I — hic — gentlemen, I appear to be — hic — under attack. The wine of last night has — hic — lodged an objection.
The god of comedy defends his title even against his own priest.

Medicine to the rescue. Hold your breath as long as you can bear. If that fails, gargle water. If THAT fails, tickle your nose with a feather and sneeze it out — one good sneeze routs a whole army of hiccups.

A feather. Up the nose. Of Athens' finest physician. — hic — Very well! Eryximachus, speak in my place while I conduct the treatment, and I shall follow you. Science first, comedy after — the natural order of any disaster.
Note it down, someone: the man who mocks the gods for a living was silenced the moment it was Love's turn to be mocked. I don't say the god did it. I only note the timing.

script.note: TO BE CONTINUED — Part Three: the doctor's speech on Love as harmony in all things — while Athens' greatest comedian sits beside him, feather in hand, waiting to deliver the strangest and most beautiful speech of the night.
